“Hell” is found in many Bible translations. In the same verses other translations read “the grave,” “the world of the dead,” and so forth. Other Bibles simply transliterate the original-language words that are sometimes rendered “hell”; that is, they express them with the letters of our alphabet but leave the words untranslated. The Hebrew she’ohlʹ and its Greek equivalent haiʹdes refer, not to an individual burial place, but to the common grave of dead mankind; also the Greek geʹen·na, which is used as a symbol of eternal destruction. In many Christian denominations it is taught that hell is a place inhabited by demons and where the wicked, after death, are punished (and some believe that this is with torment). The verses at the beginning negate torment in hell, because the dead are conscious of nothing. Therefore, the "torment" of the wicked has to occur whilest still alive: they are cast out of God's favor, and knowing that they are going to die to make room for the obedient and upright, they "weep" and "gnash their teeth".

The descriptors you list refer to geʹen·na, that is, eternal destruction. People are not "damned" to hell, as born out by Acts 2:25-27, KJ: “David speaketh concerning him [Jesus Christ], . . . Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.” That God did not “leave” Jesus in hell implies that Jesus was in hell, or Hades, at least for a time, does it not?

Thus my original statement, while requiring a qualifying clarification, remains true: Hell, in the context of "a place of torment," is not a biblical teaching. Hell is simply the common grave, oblivion, death, non-existence.
